questions.stem: Why must one first understand the existing Enterprise Data Architecture Landscape before starting a new project?
options: Because every project must introduce at least one new tool
Because every new project's data architecture must follow the existing landscape rather than introducing new components
Because regulators require a written landscape document
Because the landscape defines the project budget
questions.explanation: Every new project's data architecture must follow the existing landscape instead of adding new components with each project.

questions.stem: What is a 'Data Components / Tools Swamp'?
options: A data lake with no metadata
A network with too many switches
An organisation accumulating many tools that offer the same functionality
A database with too many indexes
A warehouse with no primary keys
questions.explanation: In the Big Data era hundreds of tools offer the same functionality, so organisations end up with a swamp of duplicate tools, described as one of the biggest risks today.

questions.stem: Which three types of architecture do most organisations confuse or mix up, which is called a recipe for disaster?
questions.explanation: Of the four architectures, most organisations mix up the last three (Data, Application and Technical); Data Architecture should remain standalone.

questions.stem: Which two components of Enterprise Data Architecture are described as very critical?
options: Enterprise Data Model and Data Flows
questions.explanation: Enterprise Data Architecture has many components, but the Enterprise Data Model and Data Flows are the two critical ones.

questions.stem: What does an Enterprise Data Model include?
options: Only the physical tables in production
Only the conceptual model agreed by the board
The network diagram of all servers
The list of approved software vendors
Conceptual, logical and physical data models with all entities, attributes, relationships and rules across the organisation
questions.explanation: The Enterprise Data Model includes conceptual, logical and physical models with all possible data points, entities, attributes, relationships and rules, agreed by all stakeholders.

questions.stem: In the Data Flows example, which process is a Product sold by?
questions.explanation: Data Flows relate entities to business processes: a Product is created by Product Development, produced by Manufacturing and sold by Order Management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the listed steps for project or product Data Architecture?
questions.explanation: The steps are Outline Architectural Scope, Business Requirement Scope, Design and Plan, and Implement; decommissioning is not among them.

questions.stem: How does the Waterfall implementation methodology proceed?
options: Sequentially, with each phase or module dependent on the previous one
In parallel sprints with an object-oriented approach
By deploying functions one at a time
By starting with the last phase first
questions.explanation: Waterfall follows a sequential implementation approach where each phase or module depends on the previous one.

questions.stem: Which methodologies are described as inherited from Agile?
questions.explanation: DevOps, DataOps and MLOps are all inherited from the Agile methodology.

questions.stem: Who drives Data Architecture and towards what does it work?
options: Data Architects, towards business value, compliance and an implementation process aligned with Enterprise Data Architecture
questions.explanation: Data Architecture is driven by Data Architects and works towards business value, compliance and implementation aligned with Enterprise Data Architecture.
